query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pulsed compression plasma flow (CPF) treatment on a tungsten precursor pre-coated with copper will promote rapid, localized melting and quenching that forms a metastable, finely mixed W(Cu) solid solution with minimized voids and phase separation, driven by severe lattice distortion, thereby improving thermal transport and irradiation tolerance compared to samples fabricated by conventional spark plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten skeleton or connected tungsten regions uniformly coated with a thin copper layer (via vapor deposition or equivalent technique) embedded within a bulk copper matrix.
generation.intervention: Expose the pre-coated tungsten sample to pulsed compression plasma flows using brief pulses and moderate energy densities to induce rapid local melting and ultra-fast quenching.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled plasma parameters at high cooling rates; service conditions include high heat flux and irradiation exposures typical of fusion reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a well-bonded, homogeneous W(Cu) interlayer featuring a fine microstructure and numerous intergranular boundaries that hinder void coalescence.
generation.mechanism: The high-intensity CPF treatment rapidly melts the copper-coated tungsten surface and, due to the extremely high cooling rates, the melted layer solidifies before significant phase separation or void formation can occur, thereby establishing a metastable W(Cu) solid solution that preserves mechanical durability and enhances thermal transport. This rapid quenching process results in severe lattice distortion, which further stabilizes the metastable phase formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional fabrication methods, the CPF-treated sample will show a denser, more uniform microstructure with fewer voids and enhanced thermal conductivity under irradiation, leading to improved overall performance as a fusion-reactor joint heat sink.
generation.baseline: Existing techniques such as spark plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or molten copper filling that often result in phase separation, void formation, or incomplete interfacial bonding.
generation.boundary: Processing boundaries include the use of CPF parameters optimized for a thin surface layer (limited to the near-surface region) and service boundaries corresponding to fusion reactor thermal and irradiation conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal CPF energy density, pulse duration, and copper coating thickness required to consistently achieve the targeted microstructure remain to be fully determined; additionally, long-term stability under combined thermal and irradiation loads is yet to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-copper composite samples: one set receiving the CPF treatment (with the specified pulse and energy parameters) and a control set fabricated by conventional methods. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature and irradiation conditions relevant to fusion reactors. Then, assess and compare their microstructural uniformity, void density, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability.
measurements: Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) for void density and phase homogeneity
X-ray diffraction (XRD) for identifying the W(Cu) solid solution formation
Thermal diffusivity and conductivity measurements via non-contact methods
Mechanical testing (e.g., shear and tensile tests) before and after irradiation exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If CPF-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in void density, improved phase uniformity, and enhanced thermal and mechanical performance compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, creating alloys based on tungsten and copper using compression plasma flows is proposed. This type of surface treatment is pulsed and allows transferring a sufficiently high energy density to the surface layer, which is necessary for its melting [,,,]. A feature of this type of treatment is the high cooling rates of the formed melt, which ensure that the processes related to the formation of the structure and phases during crystallization are non-equilibrium. Due to the high cooling rates, it is possible to achieve the condition of partial mixing of tungsten and copper in the liquid state, forming an alloy of a composite structure. In this work, it is proposed to use the effect of compression plasma flows in order to modify the structural state of the near-surface tungsten layer. Furthermore, in the case of the preliminary application of a copper coating to the surface of tungsten samples, exposure to compression plasma flows makes it possible to create an alloy based on tungsten and copper by means of their liquid-phase mixing.

Indeed, a crucial result of the pulsed treatment of the metal surfaces is a quenching effect due to the high solidification rate. When the heat transfer from the plasma stream stops, cooling of the melted layers occurs. Because of a strong correlation between the thickness of the non-molten metal part and the molten surface layer, the cooling rate can reach 106–107 K/s [,,]. The quenching effect produces an excess concentration of vacancies, which can decrease the lattice parameters of the crystal structure in the modified metals. However, the results of the effect of plasma with the same energies on pure tungsten, without any other metal as a coating, showed constant values of its lattice parameters []. Thus, it can be assumed that the presence of copper atoms in the crystal lattice of tungsten results in solid solution W(Cu) formation. The atomic radius of copper (128 pm) is less than that of tungsten (141 pm), and the formation of W(Cu) solid solution can be associated with its lattice parameter decrease. Overall, the work demonstrated the fundamental opportunity of creating alloys based on tungsten and copper by successively applying copper coating to the tungsten surface and using pulsed action of compression plasma flows with a pulse duration of 100 μs, with an absorbed energy density of 35–55 J/cm2. The results demonstrate the formation of a composite structure based on individual phases of tungsten and copper, and due to the high-speed crystallization of the molten surface layer, a solid solution of W(Cu) with a distorted crystal lattice is formed. Analysis of radiation effects during irradiation of tungsten and tungsten-copper alloy samples with helium ions with an energy of 40 keV and doses of (1–3) × 1017 cm−2 showed that tungsten samples pre-treated with CPF in the melting and mixing mode of the near-surface layer have increased radiation resistance. In the near-surface region, corresponding to the helium ion range, there is a distortion of the tungsten phase crystal lattice, which causes mechanical destruction of the surface.
